extracted.intended_audience: Wattpad users migrating to Archive of Our Own (AO3) or new AO3 users unfamiliar with AO3 tagging/culture
extracted.subtask_description: A practical guide explaining how to use tags on Archive of Our Own (AO3), covering canonical tags, relationship and crossover conventions, RPF tagging, warnings/trigger tags, and etiquette differences from Wattpad. Aims to help Wattpad authors publish fanworks on AO3 in a way that's discoverable and polite to the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical tags are searchable/filterable
rubrics_metrics.description: Canonical tags on AO3 allow you to search or filter works; selecting a tag will automatically return all works or bookmarks on the site that are using that specific tag, or the canonical tag it's been linked to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use canonical tags because they connect your work into AO3's tag system. Tags are used to specify Rating, Warnings, Fandoms, Characters, and Relationships; additional information can go in the Additional Tags section. Remember that tags on AO3 behave differently than Wattpad — they are meaningful for site-wide searching and filtering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tags are user-created keywords/phrases that inform readers
rubrics_metrics.description: A tag is a keyword/phrase that provides information about a work and can be made by anyone creating content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of tags as metadata readers use to find or avoid works. They should succinctly describe content (characters, relationships, fandoms, warnings, rating) rather than be a long stream of irrelevant keywords.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not over-tag (avoid excessively long tag lists)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do NOT tag one single work with 100 different fandoms, characters, and relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially avoid massive tag lists for one-shots or drabbles. Over-tagging is a massive headache for tag wranglers and browsing users. Nobody wants to read a mile-long tag list, particularly alongside a long summary or with no summary at all. As an anti-pattern: extremely long tags + long summary or no helpful summary = bad UX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship tag conventions: slash (/) vs ampersand (&)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relationship tag with a forward slash (/) denotes a romantic or sexual relationship. A relationship tag with an ampersand (&) denotes a familial or platonic relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Character/Character = romantic/sexual relationship (likely the main pairing or OTP). Character & Character = familial or platonic relationship, friendship. For relationships, tag the main/primary pairing the fic focuses on and secondary relationships if those are also in the fic; there is no need to tag every single relationship that appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tag primary and relevant secondary relationships only
rubrics_metrics.description: For relationships, you generally want to tag the main/primary pairing the fic focuses on, and secondary relationships if those are also in the fic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not tag every single relationship that shows up in your fanwork. Focus on those that are meaningful to the story or that readers will search for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crossover/fusion tagging conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: If your work is a crossover, tag the relevant fandoms and they will be separated with a comma; it will appear in the fandoms' tag listings and be filterable as a crossover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can also add an Additional Tag such as 'Crossover' or 'Alternate Universe - Fusion' to explicitly indicate the relationship between the fandoms in the fic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real-Person Fiction (RPF) tagging rules
rubrics_metrics.description: RPF fandoms work the same as any other fandom, except the characters are real people rather than fictional ones; tag with the appropriate fandom, usually based on the group the characters belong to, plus the RPF acronym when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the link between people is less obvious, use the group that ties them together plus 'RPF' (e.g., 'American (US) Actor RPF' when no more specific fandom applies). Do not tag fanworks about actors with the fictional-universe fandom tag; e.g., works about Jensen Ackles and Jared Padalecki should use 'Supernatural RPF' rather than 'Supernatural'. Use more general RPF tags (like 'American (US) Actor RPF') if multiple projects/roles are involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put additional warnings (triggers/kinks/squicks) in tags, not just descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are tagging for additional warnings in your story that are not covered in the Warnings section, such as potential triggers or kinks or squicks, put them IN THE TAGS, not just the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tags allow readers to filter out content they don't want to see and help readers find content they're seeking. Include clear trigger/kink tags because one person's squick is another's kink. Reminder: 'Don't Like: Don't Read. Ship and Let Ship.' Also provides a short distinction: a trigger causes PTSD-style flashbacks; a squick is something personally icky but not traumatic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Additional Tags section for extra information
rubrics_metrics.description: Further information (beyond Rating, Warnings, Fandoms, Characters, Relationships) can be added in the Additional Tags section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Additional Tags to surface elements like crossover labels, content specifics, kinks, tropes, or other metadata that help readers find or avoid your work; these are part of discoverability and community etiquette on AO3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summaries and tags should be useful — avoid minimal/no summary or overlong tag+summary combos
rubrics_metrics.description: Nobody wants to read a list of tags that's a mile long, especially if there's a long-ass summary after it (or even to get through all of that only to find there is no summary whatsoever, or it's only a single short sentence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a helpful summary and reasonable tag list. Both are important: tags for filtering/search; summary for readers to know what the work is about. Avoid the anti-patterns of either no summary or an excessive tag list combined with unnecessary verbosity.
